    <item>
      <title>Kinetic Proofreading Activation Times Beyond the Weibull Limit</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31788</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.31788v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: T cells can detect a few foreign peptide-major histocompatibility complexes (pMHCs) among a far larger number of self pMHCs. Kinetic proofreading explains this discrimination: a receptor that has bound its ligand must complete nKP signaling steps, each at rate kp, before it activates, and dissociation at any step resets its progress. When many receptors are engaged at once, the time to the first activation has been approximated by a Weibull law taken from the short-time limit of this process. The Weibull law is convenient, but it does not contain the dissociation rate koff, even though koff is what proofreading uses to tell ligands apart. Using the exact first- passage law of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain together with stochastic simulations, we show that the relative error of the Weibull law is set by a single dimensionless number {\Lambda}, the Weibull-predicted activation time measured in units of nKP + 1 bound-state lifetimes. For {\Lambda} < 1 the first receptor to activate does so before its ligand has ever dissociated, and the Weibull law holds. As {\Lambda} grows, activation relies increasingly on repeated unbinding and rebinding. The true activation time then exceeds the Weibull prediction by up to 2900-fold on our parameter grid, and the effective Weibull shape falls to one, so activation becomes memoryless instead of timer-like. We derive a closed form that keeps koff by treating the successful pass through the proofreading chain separately from the time lost to failed attempts. It matches exact medians to within 2% in 19 of 25 parameter sets, with a worst case of about 6%, and reproduces the loss of timer-like behavior. Because {\Lambda} is computed from the Weibull prediction itself, it shows in advance how far that formula can be trusted; where it cannot, the new expression requires only a one-dimensional root find.</description>

    <item>
      <title>TAPESTRY: an interactive resource for exploring tumor-enriched splice junctions in pediatric brain tumors</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31816</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.31816v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: TAPESTRY (https://tapestry.rokitalab.com) is a database and web application for exploring recurrent tumor-enriched splice junctions (TEJs) in pediatric brain tumors, cancers that carry few protein-coding mutations and therefore few mutation-derived neoantigens. However, TEJs represent a much larger source of neoantigens as potential therapeutic targets in these tumors. TAPESTRY catalogs 45,430 recurrent TEJs across 19 histologies, identified in 1,962 RNA-seq specimens (including 1,272 independent primary tumors) from the Pediatric Brain Tumor Atlas and compared to four normal brain reference cohorts comprising adult, pediatric, developmental and cell-type-resolved tissue. Each junction is classified as tumor-specific or oncofetal; annotated for splice-event type, coding consequence, novelty relative to GENCODE v39 and overlap with Pfam and UniProt protein domains; and scored for recurrence within each histology. Users can search by gene or splicing event and filter results by histology, junction class, and annotation. Users can also generate gene-level expression heatmaps across cohorts, junction-level expression boxplots, and transcript and exon diagrams, and download all tables and figures. A documented REST API supports programmatic access, and all source code is openly available. By making tumor-selective and developmentally reactivated splicing events searchable and interpretable, TAPESTRY supports the prioritization of splice-derived targets for antibody-based, cell-based and vaccine immunotherapies in pediatric brain and central nervous system tumors.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Phase-based Edge Coupling: Modeling Overlapping Functional Architectures and High-Order Edge-to-Edge Interactions in EEG Networks</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32286</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32286v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Network neuroscience has traditionally relied on node-centric approaches, which are inherently limited in capturing the brain's overlapping functional architectures and higher-order edge-to-edge interactions. The emerging edge-centric paradigm addresses this gap by shifting the analytical unit from nodes to edges. However, while edge-centric models have been established for DTI and fMRI, comparable EEG methodologies have yet to be developed. In this study, we proposed a Phase-based Edge-centric Coupling (PEC) algorithm for EEG network modelling, where edge time series are derived from instantaneous phase differences of EEG signals and edge-to-edge coupling is quantified via normalized inner product. Simulation tests demonstrated the robustness of PEC algorithm, achieving high accuracy (<10% relative error) in coupling estimation and discriminative capacity (AUROC>0.7) against spurious coupling.When provided sufficient data length(>=16 cycles), PEC outperformed traditional Phase Node-centric Coupling (PNC) in both individual identifiability and cognitive-state identifiability, enabling superior characterization of stable individual neural signatures and dynamic task-dependent functional configurations. Furthermore, unlike PNC's hard-partitioned modularity, PEC captured highly overlapping yet functionally specialized modular structures and connector hubs, aligning with task-engaged cognitive processes. Applied to dyadic interactions, PEC identified distinct cross-brain modules encoding symmetric and asymmetric neural coordination. These findings establish PEC as a valid and powerful tool for EEG network modelling, providing new insights into the brain's complex, multifunctional organization at both intra-brain and inter-brain networks.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Dynamics of a Harvested Predator-Prey Model with a Generalized Holling Type~III Response Capturing Group Defense</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32306</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32306v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate a predator-prey model with constant prey harvesting and a generalized Holling type III functional response, focusing on the biological and dynamical consequences of allowing the parameter $b$ to be negative. In this regime, predation efficiency declines at high prey densities, potentially reflecting group defense. This change permits an additional coexistence equilibrium and introduces new bifurcation mechanisms affecting population persistence. We establish the existence of a codimension-three Bogdanov--Takens bifurcation, derive a codimension-three nilpotent-saddle unfolding, and investigate a codimension-two generalized Hopf bifurcation and the emergence of multiple limit cycles. Our analysis show that moderate harvesting weakens the protection conferred by high prey abundance; excessive harvesting leaves too few prey to sustain predator growth; and low harvesting preserves strong group defense, requiring high predator density for population persistence.</description>

    <item>
      <title>From Heterogeneity to Function: Enhanced Modular Dynamic Range in Hierarchical Brain Networks</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32328</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32328v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Hierarchical and modular organization defines brain architecture, yet how it supports flexible computation and functional specialization remains unclear. Although dynamic range is a hallmark of efficient information processing, its distribution across modules and hierarchical levels remains largely unexplored. Here, we show that hierarchical-modular networks naturally generate heterogeneous modular dynamics and firing rates, extending regimes of critical-like dynamics with enhanced intrinsic timescales, reflecting critical slowing down, and diverse scaling exponents without fine-tuning near criticality. Intrinsic timescales increase across hierarchical levels, while their dispersion within levels emerges only when connectivity profiles and firing rates are heterogeneous. We introduce modular dynamic range to quantify how individual modules respond to external inputs and show that heterogeneity enhances both global and module-specific sensitivity, with modular intrinsic timescales increasing with dynamic range. Local stimulation reduces dynamic range in homogeneous networks but enhances it in heterogeneous networks relative to global stimulation. Moreover, selectively stimulating intermediate hierarchical levels maximizes both global and modular dynamic range, revealing a principle of functional specialization. In heterogeneous networks, modular dynamic range is more variable and increases even in unstimulated modules, demonstrating distributed computational benefits beyond directly stimulated regions. Together, these findings establish heterogeneity as a mechanism through which hierarchical-modular networks sustain critical-like dynamics, generate hierarchical timescales, and distribute computational sensitivity, providing a basis for functional specialization without fine-tuning to criticality.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Stochastic predator-prey compartment model with cyclic and non-cyclic transition pathways and mortality</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32535</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32535v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study variants of a stochastic SEIRS-SEID compartmental model incorporating presymptomatic infectiousness and disease-related mortality, with independent compartmental sojourn times drawn from arbitrary distributions, in particular Weibull distributions. We consider a large population of agents that occupy the states (compartments) S (susceptible to infection), E (exposed: infected but asymptomatic during the latency period and already infectious, including diseases with presymptomatic infections), I (infected and infectious, with symptoms), R (recovered, immune, and non-infectious), or D (dead). We consider (i) cyclic transmission pathways, where compartmental sojourn times are finite and immunity is temporary, and (ii) non-cyclic pathways, where immunity is permanent. In the absence of mortality, cyclic transmission pathways support an endemic equilibrium above the spreading threshold which is either globally stable or oscillatory (Hopf) unstable, whereas for non-cyclic pathways a stationary disease-free state is emerging. From a stochastic perspective, we elucidate the connection between compartmental sojourn-time distributions and the appearance of fractional operators in the evolution equations: fat-tailed compartment waiting-time distributions necessarily lead to fractional derivatives. For cyclic transition pathways we obtain an explicit expression for the expected number of infection cycles that an agent survives. Our model is validated by a combined Monte Carlo -- Runge -- Kutta simulation scheme and random-walk simulations on Barabasi-Albert networks. It has cross-disciplinary applications beyond epidemiology, including wildfire spreading, certain classes of chemical reactions, population dynamics, finance, economics, and biology.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Estimation of the Cyclopean Eye from Binocular Free Visual Explorations</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32564</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Binocular video-oculography records separate signals for each eye, yet human visual processing and oculomotor control operate relative to a single, virtual cyclopean eye. This study addresses the estimation of the cyclopean eye during binocular free visual exploration, a target-free paradigm widely used for the screening of neurological disorders. Using eye-tracking data collected at 1 kHz from 113 participants across three cohorts (patients with Parkinson's Disease, age-matched healthy controls, and young controls), we compare two different methods: one based on an Independent Component Analysis and another based on Factor Analysis. The extracted cyclopean signals were evaluated on their ability to preserve clinically critical fixation and saccadic events using both velocity-threshold and pixel-dispersion event detectors, and were validated against references via Dynamic Time Warping. Results suggest that the technique based on Factor Analysis guarantees full identifiability across all subjects and achieves low alignment errors, performing comparably to the traditional Version Signal (point-wise mean) while dynamically adapting to inter-eye asymmetry. Furthermore, the second factor in this technique was empirically null across all fitted models, confirming that a single latent factor fully accounts for the shared binocular gaze dynamics. These findings establish Factor Analysis as an identifiable framework for estimating the cyclopean eye in target-free visual exploration protocols.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Computational De Novo Design of Miniprotein Candidate Neutralizers Targeting the IL-23 Cytokine Subunit p19</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32779</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32779v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Interleukin-23 (IL-23) drives T-helper-17 inflammation underlying inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis; anti-p19 antibodies are clinically effective but large, costly, and injectable. De novo miniproteins are an attractive alternative, yet published designs target the IL-23 receptor; the IL-23 cytokine itself has not been addressed. A further obstacle is that the standard confidence score (ipTM) tracks construct length rather than interface quality. We computationally design miniprotein binders against the IL-23R-binding face of p19 (PDB 3DUH) and score every design with ipSAE, a length-robust interface metric derived from AlphaFold-initial-guess predicted aligned error. A conventional RFdiffusion/ProteinMPNN/ColabFold pipeline yields no reliable predicted interface across 972 designs (best ipSAE 0.30), and a scoring artifact, in which single-sequence ColabFold under-rates binder pLDDT by approximately 56 points, explains an earlier misleading "binders do not fold" signal. An interface-optimized hallucination method (BindCraft), scored identically, yields 42 of 50 designs above ipSAE 0.60 (best 0.804). An AlphaFold-independent geometric check reproduces the conventional failure: no top-ranked conventional design reaches the buried area or interface hydrogen-bond count of the weakest lead. Five all-alpha-helical leads (72-104 residues) collectively engage all six targeted hotspots; two dock within the intact p40/p19 heterodimer and all show favorable Rosetta energetics. A p40-alone counter-screen returns ipSAE 0.00 for all five, indicating no spurious p40 interface. To our knowledge, these are the first computationally proposed de novo miniprotein candidates designed to occlude the IL-23R-binding face of IL-23 p19. All results require experimental validation.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Shared clones make random cell halves look reproducible in pooled screens</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32962</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32962v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Single-cell perturbation screens are used to train and evaluate models that predict perturbation effects, and model scores are judged against how reproducible the measured effects are. Reproducibility is usually judged by splitting each perturbation's cells into two random halves. This assumes that the halves are independent replicates. In pooled screens such as Perturb-seq, however, the cells carrying a guide RNA descend from a limited number of transduced cells, so two random halves contain the same clones: pseudoreplication whose unit is not marked in the data. Using perturbations that should have no effect as controls, we compared random halves with independent replicates from separate transductions, and tested directly with halves that differ only in their clones. In a genome-scale screen of primary T cells, null perturbations agreed between random halves almost always and between independent replicates only half the time, the rate expected from noise alone; measuring more cells did not remove this agreement. Splitting the cells into halves that share no clone, by the T-cell receptor constant region or by a clone barcode, largely removed the excess agreement. Its size equals the share of expression differences set by clones divided by the effective number of clones per perturbation; across 16 screens it was largest in T cells transferred into mice and in a genome-scale primary T-cell screen, one to two orders of magnitude smaller in cell lines, and smallest in non-dividing neurons. Shared clones inflate benchmark ceilings and reliability labels, and when a model's input and its scoring answer come from one transduction, published models that predict perturbation effects in a new cell state appear better than a baseline that ignores the perturbation; against cells from another transduction, most fall below it. Reproducibility should be judged across separate transductions.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Post-transcriptional Regulation of Stochastic Gene Expression Conditioned on Large Deviations</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17004</link>
      <description>arXiv:2607.17004v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Gene expression is a stochastic process that gives rise to large fluctuations in protein levels leading to phenotypic heterogeneity in clonal cell populations; post-transcriptional regulation plays a crucial role in controlling the level of phenotypic variability within a population, which is directly tied to cell-fate decisions. As such, substantial efforts have been directed towards quantitatively modeling the effects of various post-transcriptional mechanisms on the strength of fluctuations in protein levels (noise). However, the corresponding effects of post-transcriptional regulation on the occurrence of rare events corresponding to large deviations are far less explored and have only been considered for a special model. Here, we take a general model of post-transcriptional regulation and apply the partitioning of Poisson arrivals (PPA) framework to map it onto a model that resembles promoter-based regulation of transcription, leading to a general framework to obtain objects of interest in large deviations (i.e. large deviation rate function for quantifying the likelihood of observing rare protein production rates and the corresponding driven process that characterizes the system dynamics conditional on the rare event) for models of post-transcriptional regulation directly from prior results for promoter-based models. The results derived create new avenues to analyze rare events in general models of post-transcriptional regulation pertaining to various different biological settings.</description>

    <item>
      <title>A Mathematical Theory of the Jacobian Lens</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31955</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.31955v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Recent work from Anthropic introduced a new interpretability tool, called the Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al., 2026). This method identified linear directions in the hidden states of frontier language models that had properties reminiscent of working memory-like representations. However, it is unclear what mechanistic properties of such features make them detectable to the J-lens. To this end, we introduce a mathematical theory of the J-lens, and show that it preferentially identifies coherent features -- directions that act like leading, spatially coherent Lyapunov modes. Small perturbations along these directions amplify across layers, remain roughly constant across token positions, and are consistent across different contexts. While we are agnostic to whether these properties are necessarily associated with a ``Global Workspace'', the analytically derived preferences of the J-lens nevertheless explain prior empirical applied to both model classes. We validate our analysis on a Bayes filter and a toy transformer, each optimally predicting next tokens emitted from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show how modulating task parameters that change the coherence of features in the Bayes filter correspondingly and predictively modulates the response of the J-lens . We also introduce of a family of J-lenses built to emphasize different temporal scales of information processing in LLMs, which we call $\omega$-J-lenses.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Virtual Placebo: a scoping review of control conditions in randomized controlled trials of psychological immersive virtual reality interventions</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32232</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32232v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Research on immersive virtual reality (IVR) as a therapeutic tool is growing rapidly, with randomized controlled trials (RCTs) now commonplace. Yet the control conditions in many of these studies that claim strong specific IVR effects vary from usual care to active immersive experiences, making it difficult to draw clinically meaningful conclusions. We conducted a scoping review of recent literature on psychological IVR interventions to assess the main forms of control conditions used and their relations to study outcomes. In this paper, we make the case that most of the recent RCTs studying the effects of specific IVR interventions compare active immersive VR to usual care with no multimedia component. This can lead to strong yet potentially misleading study outcomes and can potentially inflate the IVR interventions' effect. Namely, the lack of an appropriate immersive control condition may risk misattributing general effects of VR devices to the specific content of the intervention. In this review, we discuss the implications of these design choices and propose strategies for including a suitable "virtual placebo" condition to improve the methodological rigor and interpretability of results.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Earth embeddings are decomposable records of the land surface</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32617</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32617v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Ecological monitoring, carbon accounting and biodiversity assessment increasingly rely on annual Earth embeddings--learned vectors that compress a year of satellite observation for every ten-meter pixel on Earth, consumed in place of the imagery itself. What these vectors mean has not been established. Here we decompose two widely used embedding products and show that they contain individual ecological features, including fire, forest clearing and crop type, validated against independent reference data on events across six continents. The recovered concepts date abrupt canopy loss to the first post-disturbance growing season and resolve severity well enough to separate prescribed fire from wildfire. Small fires that recover quickly are detectable in one product but not the other, which instead separates crops more strongly.</description>

    <item>
      <title>What Transfers Across Protein Pockets? Experience Reuse in Molecular Optimization for Agentic Structure-Based Drug Design</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32620</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32620v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: LLM agents optimize a ligand in a protein pocket by editing it step by step and docking each edit. Recent agents first spend extra dockings probing the complex with controlled edits; guidance induced from these probes is reported to help more than the chemical knowledge the model already carries. The probes are then discarded with the instance that produced them, so the obvious next step is to keep them in an experience base, letting a new pocket inherit what earlier ones already paid for. Such a base is read through a \emph{key}: the record properties under which past edits are pooled and a new one is looked up. Using the full log of one such run over the CrossDocked2020 test-set pockets, we ask whether its keys recur on a pocket the base has never seen and still separate improving from worsening edits. \crchange{Using} the contacts at the site being edited, the action, and the round as \crchange{a} key, the base separates them sharply. Within our analysis, this separation is largely explained by how much the edit changed the molecule's size, the action, and the round, none of which describes the target. That is not because the target is irrelevant: naming it outright separates them several times more sharply. For a pocket absent from the base, transfer must rely on a description rather than its identity. Among the exact-match descriptions we evaluate, the more specific ones rarely recur, whereas the coarser ones provide little separation; the signals that do transfer primarily describe the edit and the molecule it produced rather than the target. Under the representations and lookup scheme studied here, an experience base may be more useful for prioritizing an agent's own proposals for docking than for directly prescribing what to build.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Video-rate quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging (QP2I) for label-free imaging of contracting muscle cells</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32756</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32756v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) has become a standard approach for label-free microscopy of transparent specimens, mapping the optical path length. However, the isotropic phase is blind to the molecular order underlying optical anisotropy. Implementations that also add quantitative contrast to birefringence, rely on multi-frame illumination or polarization-state scanning, or on dedicated interferometric hardware, that trade away acquisition speed or the simplicity of a standard microscope. We present Quantitative Phase and Polarimetric Imaging (QP2I), a computational imaging framework that converts a standard differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope with a polarization camera into a single-shot, video-rate, dual-contrast imaging system. We developed a new globally regularized phase reconstruction that eliminates artifacts of prior DIC-to-QPI approaches, providing quantitative phase information and used per-pixel Stokes-based reconstruction to obtain quantitative anisotropic retardance. We validate the approach across simulations, static reference targets, fixed muscle tissue and living dynamically moving cells. Thereby, QP2I enables to study contractile dynamics in live cardiomyocytes all-optically and label-free. It provides both structural and functional readouts at frame rates that are sufficient to temporally resolve fast cardiomyocyte contractions. While conventional fluorescent labels bleach out over time, perturb physiology, and preclude long-term monitoring, QP2I provides similar established structural readouts, such as frame-by-frame sarcomere length, as well as previously inaccessible measurements, like quantitative analysis of retardance changes during muscle contraction, as a direct optical signature of muscle photoelasticity. QP2I thus enables long-term, label-free interrogation of dynamic cellular processes at quantitative contrast.</description>

    <item>
      <title>ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32926</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32926v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Zakai Equation Neural Operator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO's ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized \textit{C. elegans} nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory.</description>

      <title>A Central Limit Theorem for the Driver Site Frequency Spectrum</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32942</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.32942v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We consider a supercritical two-type continuous-time linear birth-death process with mutation and selection, in which wild-type individuals give rise to mutant offspring with a larger net-growth rate. We previously had obtained first-order law of large number results for the driver site frequency spectrum. We return to obtain a second-order central limit theorem, in which we show stable convergence of a scaling of the deviation of the SFS from its first-order limit. We provide a central limit theorem at both large detection times and sizes. Then, we apply these results to obtain confidence intervals for a class of consistent estimators for the fitness advance.</description>

      <title>Hodge-Decomposition of Brain Networks</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10542</link>
      <description>arXiv:2211.10542v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We analyze brain networks by decomposing them into three orthogonal components: gradient, curl, and harmonic flows, through the Hodge decomposition, a technique advantageous for capturing complex topological features. A Wasserstein distance based topological inference is developed to determine the statistical significance of each component. Our results indicate statistically significant differences in the topological features between male and female brain networks.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Detecting absence: A dedicated prediction-error signal emerging in the auditory thalamus</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21605</link>
      <description>arXiv:2511.21605v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: How does the brain know what is out there and what is not? Living organisms cannot rely solely on sensory signals for perception because they are noisy and ambiguous. To form stable percepts, the brain exploits its prior knowledge or beliefs. Current theories explain how perceptual beliefs on the features of the stimuli (e.g., pitch or motion velocity) are updated by feature prediction errors: the mismatch between expected and observed values. How the brain updates beliefs about a stimulus' presence or absence is, however, unclear.
  Previous work has argued that detecting absence, which relies on the lack of evidence for presence, depends on different mechanisms than the identification of a feature. Here, we tested the hypothesis that the detection of absence relies on a form of prediction error dedicated to the update of beliefs on stimulus occurrence. Since feature prediction error already occurs in the sensory pathway, we hypothesised that this would be similar for absence prediction error. We studied this absence prediction error in the human auditory pathway with fMRI by measuring BOLD responses to absence of stimuli for which the participants held different levels of expectations.
  Comparing more and less expected responses to absence, we showed that prediction error to absence is represented in the auditory thalamus and cortex. Moreover, while feature prediction error is encoded in the auditory midbrain, absence prediction error was not, implying that absence is processed by a different circuit. These results identify the neural mechanism for the detection of sensory absence. These mechanisms may be disrupted in conditions like psychosis, where the detection of absence is impaired.</description>

      <title>Convex Analysis of Relaxation Dynamics in Chemical Reaction Networks and Generalized Gradient Flows</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18932</link>
      <description>arXiv:2602.18932v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We obtain bounds on the Kullback--Leibler divergence to equilibrium for mass-action chemical reaction networks (CRNs) with equilibrium. The associated trajectory-dependent bounds are characterized in terms of the singular values of the stoichiometric matrix, convexity parameters, and time-integrated activities via deformed-exponential-type functions. We further extend these bounds within a generalized gradient flow framework. We highlight the biological relevance of this framework: the resulting bounds apply to quasi-steady-state regimes, where long transients and plateau-like behavior are common and functionally important. We illustrate the framework using a catalytic CRN exhibiting plateaus, where the bounds provide an a posteriori characterization of slow relaxation induced by local convexity and provide a bound-based approach to quantifying relaxation in CRNs.</description>

      <title>A Multiscale Kinetic Model of DNA Damage Signalling and Repair under Combined Proton and Nanoparticle Exposure</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29157</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.29157v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We present a multiscale kinetic framework for predicting the induction, processing, and biological consequences of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in AG1522 human fibroblasts exposed to combined proton and 15-nm GNP irradiation. The model connects proton dose and linear energy transfer (LET), perinuclear GNP localization, secondary-electron and reactive-species production, and Poisson--Gamma-distributed lesion induction. Initial DSBs are separated into simple and complex classes and coupled to an ATM--$\gamma$H2AX--53BP1 signalling cascade, cell-cycle-dependent allocation among canonical non-homologous end joining, homologous recombination, alternative end joining, and single-strand annealing, and class-specific repair fidelities. The model identifies the initial complex-lesion fraction and its slower resolution, rather than post-irradiation conversion of simple DSBs, as the principal determinants of persistent damage under high-LET, GNP-enhanced irradiation. The residual-DSB results provide strong internal out-of-sample validation of the kinetic component. However, the opposing biases in correct repair and misrepair reveal an inconsistency between the class-specific fidelities and the supplied integrated-fidelity endpoint. These repair-fate predictions should therefore be regarded as model-constrained estimates pending independent measurements of correct-end joining, mutation, chromosome aberrations, and clonogenic survival.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Probe Before You Edit: Probing-Guided Molecular Optimization for LLM Agents in Structure-Based Drug Design</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00555</link>
      <description>arXiv:2606.00555v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Structure-based drug design increasingly employs LLM agents to iteratively refine ligands against a target pocket, yet a viable ligand must satisfy two often-conflicting objectives---binding affinity and druggability---which single optimization steps rarely improve together. To quantify this difficulty, we introduce two diagnostic metrics: the first measures how often a single edit improves both objectives, and the second measures how often a gain on one objective comes with a loss on the other. Applying these diagnostics to current LLM-agent pipelines exposes a consistent failure mode: the agent performs molecular editing without knowing how the pocket-ligand complex responds to local modifications, thus rarely achieving joint improvement. Inspired by medicinal chemists, who probe the pocket-ligand complex with controlled analog edits before choosing an optimization direction, we propose \textbf{PROBE}, an optimization framework built around edit--response probing. PROBE first decomposes the ligand into editable sites and builds a pocket-specific \textbf{site map} that flags where joint gains are plausible, where the two objectives are likely in tension, and where liability substructures should be changed; it then performs controlled probe edits whose responses are distilled into an \textbf{EditManual}. Guided by the site map and EditManual, PROBE runs an iterative multi-agent optimization loop. On the CrossDocked2020 benchmark, PROBE achieves state-of-the-art performance and substantially mitigates the failure modes exposed by our diagnostics metrics. Codes are in https://github.com/yzf-code/PROBE/tree/main</description>

    <item>
      <title>AI-guided deep visual proteomics reveals recurrence-associated morpho-molecular signatures within triple-negative breast cancers</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03145</link>
      <description>arXiv:2608.03145v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Outcome informed AI can localize prognostically relevant regions in digital pathology, but directly characterizing the molecular basis of these spatial predictions remains challenging. Here, we developed an outcome informed, AI-guided deep visual proteomics framework that uses recurrence-risk heatmaps to guide physical tissue sampling and mass spectrometry-based spatial proteomics in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). In 156 patients, high- and low-risk regions coexisted within the tumor compartment and showed distinct nuclear and architectural features, indicating intratumoral variation beyond broad tissue identity. Guided by these maps, we physically isolated and profiled 46 AI-defined high- and low-risk tumor regions from two recurrent cases. High-risk regions were enriched for mitotic programs, whereas low-risk regions showed immune- and antigen-presentation-associated programs. We used proteins that consistently differed between high- and low-risk regions to construct a 13-protein composite. The composite showed a significant effect to discriminate highly recurrent patients from less recurrent patients in an expanded TNBC cohort, while the corresponding transcript-based score showed a similar trend in METABRIC. Integrating the protein composite with the H&E-derived risk score improved out-of-bag discrimination, increasing the C-index from 0.679 to 0.739 and the 5-year time-dependent AUC from 0.675 to 0.770. These findings establish outcome-informed H&E risk maps as spatial guides for molecular discovery, extending prognostic AI from prediction toward direct biological interrogation of recurrence-associated tissue states.</description>

    <item>
      <title>GenAIT: Development and Validation of an Objective Generative AI Literacy Test for High School Students</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25815</link>
      <description>arXiv:2608.25815v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: There is growing international interest in generative AI (GenAI) literacy and its assessment among high school students, but objective assessment in this population remains underdeveloped. This article reports the iterative development and validation of the GenAI Literacy Test (GenAIT), an 18-item multiple-choice test measuring high school students' conceptual knowledge about GenAI, with content spanning technical, practical, and human-impact domains. Expert review of relevance, clarity, and comprehensiveness provided evidence of content validity. In a large-scale survey of 7432 Estonian high school students, we evaluated the psychometric functioning of the Estonian-language GenAIT using confirmatory factor analysis, classical test theory, and item response theory. Results supported approximate unidimensionality, broadly adequate reliability for group-level research (marginal reliability = .72, KR-20 = .69), and good fit of a three-parameter logistic model (RMSEA = .013, TLI = .987, CFI = .990, SRMSR = .021). Measurement precision was sufficient for the majority of students but varied substantially across the latent trait, with lower precision for lower scoring students. GenAIT is therefore more suitable for group-level research than high-stakes individual classification. GenAIT scores were unrelated to perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, and negatively associated with LLM use frequency, suggesting that frequent use and favorable perceptions of AI should not be treated as proxies for conceptual understanding.</description>

      <title>HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25898</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.25898v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns in continuous recordings. Repeated template reconstruction and correlation evaluation make analyses across recordings and parameter settings computationally expensive. We present HP-GSBS, an open-source implementation that expresses the matching objective as additive interval contributions and computes t-distance from reusable correlation statistics. Streaming candidate reduction, sequential local refinement, and active-block reuse complement CPU, PyTorch CUDA, and Triton execution paths. Across seven controlled workloads with two input realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154 to 1,730. All 168 optimized executions reproduce complete reference boundary histories and selected state counts, with a maximum absolute t-distance difference of $1.88\times10^{-11}$. Four publicly supplied BBBD EEG analysis matrices provide complementary cross-backend validation. A naturalistic fMRI application segments 4,230 angular-gyrus voxels in a group response and 16 participants; the 17 CPU fits total 213.10 seconds. Mean pairwise boundary alignment exceeds a circular-shift baseline, illustrating cohort-level use of the saved segmentations. Versioned results, recording-level parallelism, and optional low-memory execution support varied analysis scales. HP-GSBS connects an explicit mathematical reformulation of repeated computation to efficient and reproducible neural-state analysis.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Bio-Inspired Auditory Processing: Coupling Parallel Resonate-and-Fire Dynamics with Ternary Recurrent Networks for Speech Recognition</title>
      <link>https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29720</link>
      <description>arXiv:2610.29720v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient inference through sparse, event-driven computation, yet remain constrained on continuous, context-dependent tasks such as automatic speech recognition (ASR). A key bottleneck is the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron, whose membrane decay erases information across pauses and phonetic boundaries while it must both extract features and retain long-range context. Inspired by cortical separation of nonlinear filtering and somatic integration, we introduce the Spiking Ternary GRU (stGRU): a ternary-weight gated recurrent unit performs temporal filtering, while downstream Resonate-and-Fire (RF) neurons generate the binary spike stream driving the next block's event pathway. This makes binary event transmission a native training constraint rather than a separate deployment-time activation quantization step; together with ternary weights, learned projections avoid dense floating-point matrix MACs. Trained end-to-end on LibriSpeech-960, Small, Medium, and Large stGRUs reach 8.09%, 7.04%, and $6.44 \pm 0.17\%$ WER on test-clean without an external language model. To our knowledge, these are the first matrix-MAC-free spiking networks without a learned ANN sequence decoder to achieve single-digit WER on LibriSpeech. The architecture also achieves 10.88% test CER on Aishell-1 (9.28% on dev) when trained from scratch. Internally, trained networks develop a depth-graded hierarchy: shallow layers act as fast acoustic filters, while deep layers form slower semantic integrators whose latent representations segregate into part-of-speech manifolds and word-level spike events. Deep-layer firing rates follow lognormal distributions with a sparsity gradient, mirroring hierarchical processing observed in human cortex in vivo. Our biologically grounded architecture combines competitive ASR with favorable modeled compute and memory cost.</description>
